highlights: Clifftop Northland sanctuary with Pacific views, private beaches and championship golf
description:
Rosewood Kauri Cliffs occupies a dramatic coastal estate above Matauri Bay in Northland, where the Bay of Islands gives way to open Pacific horizons, Cape Brett and the Cavalli Islands. The resort sits on a 6,000-acre working farm and forested headland, placing Kerikeri, Waitangi’s historic Māori and colonial sites, secluded coves and the beaches of the far north within reach, while the immediate mood is one of deep rural seclusion rather than conventional resort polish.

The 26-key retreat is arranged as 22 suites and four villas around a main lodge, with accommodations set among native bush and looking across the golf course, farmland and water. Interiors have a New Zealand lodge character softened by contemporary restraint: timber, stone, fireplaces, generous verandas and a palette designed to keep attention on the landscape. The larger villas add residential privacy, pools and broad terraces for families or groups.

Dining is centred on Northland produce, New Zealand lamb, seafood, native herbs and estate-grown ingredients, served in the lodge or arranged as private meals in wilder corners of the property. The sense of place is sharpened by the David Harman-designed par-72 championship golf course, which rolls over cliffs and pasture with sea views from many holes.

Wellness has a strongly outdoor rhythm: a spa set among native forest, indoor lap pool, Jacuzzi, outdoor pool and hot tub, sauna facilities, fitness centre, tennis and pickleball courts, trails and guided cultural or nature experiences. Three private beaches below the cliffs, fishing, boating, stargazing and forest walks make the estate feel less like a hotel than a private Northland landscape opened selectively to guests.

local_area: Plaza de las Cortes / Landscape of Light
highlights: Restored Belle Époque landmark beneath Madrid’s iconic stained-glass dome
description:
The Palace stands on Plaza de las Cortes facing the Neptuno Fountain, in Madrid’s UNESCO-listed Landscape of Light and within walking distance of the Prado, Thyssen-Bornemisza and Reina Sofía museums. The address places the hotel between the Cortes, Barrio de las Letras and Paseo del Prado, close to the Royal Botanical Garden, Retiro Park, Gran Vía and the city’s central galleries, theatres and restaurants.

Opened in 1912 and extensively renewed for its new era as The Luxury Collection, the hotel remains one of Madrid’s great social landmarks. Its 470 renovated guestrooms and suites retain a grand-hotel scale, while interiors by Lázaro Rosa-Violán draw on local history, botanical references and the long roster of artists, writers and statesmen associated with the building. Restored marble, period columns, custom artworks and historic detailing keep the renovation anchored in the Palace’s original Belle Époque character.

At the heart of the hotel is La Cúpula Restaurant & Bar, set beneath the restored stained-glass dome. The restaurant serves Spanish cooking shaped by Madrid references and historic guest stories, while the circular bar brings a more contemporary rhythm to the monumental room with cocktails, tapas and an extensive wine list. Beside it, 27 Club nods to the poets, artists and intellectuals who helped define the hotel’s cultural mythology.

Facilities include a 24-hour fitness area, wellness treatments on request, room service and substantial meeting and event spaces, making the property as much a civic salon as a place to stay. Its strongest amenity, however, is location: a restored Madrid institution embedded directly in the city’s museum district.

highlights: Secluded old-town convent with Roman baths, terraced gardens and Riviera light
description:
Hôtel du Couvent sits behind quiet walls in Vieux Nice, at the foot of the hill rising toward the city’s old castle park, with the lanes of the old town, Place Rossetti, Cours Saleya, the port and the Promenade des Anglais all within easy reach. The Mediterranean is close enough to shape the light, yet the atmosphere inside the former 17th-century convent is unusually hushed for central Nice.

The 88 rooms and suites occupy a restored religious complex set among cloistered courtyards and gardens, with interiors that favor lime plaster, terracotta, old stone, antique pieces and a monastic clarity softened for contemporary comfort. Some accommodations open to terraces or gardens, and the best frame old-town rooftops or the distant horizon. The renovation preserves the feeling of a layered building rather than smoothing it into a conventional Riviera hotel.

Food and drink unfold across bars, terraces and restaurants, with Le 1604 rooted in local produce and the ritual of cooking around the cloister. A bakery, herbalist’s corner, kitchen garden and market-minded sensibility reinforce the sense that the hotel is part retreat, part neighbourhood institution. The terraced grounds, shaped with Mediterranean planting, lead toward a slim outdoor lap pool and pockets of shade.

Wellness is central to the hotel’s identity. The Roman Baths and Movement Studio cover about 7,500 square feet, combining thermal bathing, treatments, Pilates, yoga and restorative movement, while indoor and outdoor pools add rare resort-style depth to an old-town address. Cultural programming, family activities and easy access to the beach give Hôtel du Couvent a distinctive balance: contemplative, design-conscious and deeply anchored in Nice.

highlights: Art Deco Mayfair hideaway with Hyde Park views and Michelin-starred omakase
description:
45 Park Lane occupies a polished Mayfair address directly opposite Hyde Park, a short walk from The Dorchester, Mount Street, Shepherd Market, Bond Street and the galleries and boutiques that define this part of London’s West End. Its scale is deliberately intimate for Park Lane: a contemporary sister to the grand hotel across the road, with the park’s treetops and the London skyline as its constant backdrop.

With just 45 rooms and suites, including a penthouse, the hotel feels closer to a private townhouse than a traditional London palace. Every room overlooks Hyde Park, while higher floors open broader views across the city. Thierry W. Despont’s Art Deco-inspired interiors use rich woods, chrome, leather, warm tones and major contemporary art to create a club-like atmosphere, sharpened by works associated with the hotel’s Art at 45 Park Lane programme.

Dining gives the address unusual depth. CUT at 45 Park Lane, Wolfgang Puck’s first European restaurant, brings American steakhouse energy to a double-height room, now led by chef Elliott Grover with a focus on carefully sourced British produce. Bar 45 adds cocktails and a serious wine collection, while Sushi Kanesaka offers a hidden 13-seat omakase counter from Shinji Kanesaka’s Ginza tradition. The restaurant holds one Michelin star in the 2026 Michelin Guide United Kingdom, giving the hotel a discreet but exceptional Japanese dining dimension.

Wellness is supported by access to a subterranean spa, swimming pool, treatments, gym and personal training, while Hyde Park provides the simplest daily ritual: a morning walk, run or ride just outside the door. For such a central London location, the combination of compact scale, art, park views and serious dining feels notably composed.

highlights: Georgian Berkshire estate with polo fields, wildflower meadows and Michelin-starred dining
description:
Coworth Park lies in Sunningdale on the edge of Windsor Great Park, a few miles from Ascot Racecourse and within easy reach of Windsor, Eton and Heathrow. The 240-acre estate gives the Dorchester Collection a rare country-house address: close enough to London for a weekend, yet surrounded by meadows, woodland, grazing horses and the unmistakable rituals of English sporting life.

The hotel is centred on an 18th-century Georgian mansion, with 70 guest rooms and suites spread through the main house, converted stables and cottages across the estate. Interiors balance country comfort with contemporary polish, using pale tones, equestrian cues, four-poster beds, fireplaces and freestanding copper baths in many categories. Larger houses and cottage-style suites give families and longer-stay guests a more private version of the same pastoral setting.

Food is a major part of the stay. Woven by Adam Smith, set within the hotel, holds one Michelin star in the 2026 Michelin Guide United Kingdom and presents modern British cooking with a refined sense of produce and memory. The Barn provides a more relaxed estate restaurant, while The Drawing Room keeps the country-house tradition of afternoon tea and fireside drinks alive.

Beyond the mansion, Coworth Park’s facilities are unusually complete for an English rural hotel. The spa is partly sunken into the landscape and includes treatment rooms, an indoor pool, gym and café, while the equestrian centre, polo fields, tennis courts, bikes, walking routes and family activities make the grounds central rather than decorative. The hotel’s most distinctive quality is this blend of polished Dorchester service with genuine estate life, from riding lessons to meadow walks before dinner.
